title: At the foot of the cross (John 19:25–30)
hookLine: his mother stands there, and he gives her and John to each other

cards: At a hospital bed there can come a point where there's nothing left to do. No more phone calls, no more questions for the doctor. Just being there.
Staying. Outside Jerusalem is a place John calls Golgotha, the place of a skull, and a Roman cross. Over it hangs the title Pilate wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.
Standing near a man Rome was executing under that title can't have been safe. But John says a small group stands near the cross anyway.

teach.h: THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS HIS MOTHER.
teach.b: John names them, in the King James Bible: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene."
Mostly women, and one man John never names, only calls the disciple whom Jesus loved; Christian tradition has long said this was John himself.
And there is Mary, his mother: the one who said let it be to the angel, who wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, who heard Simeon say a sword would pierce her own soul. Now she's here.
Jesus, in terrible pain, looks down and takes care of her.
"Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And John says: "And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home."
Even on the cross he's making sure his mother won't be alone. Some read more here too: Catholics and Orthodox Christians often see Mary given as a mother to every disciple.
Then he says: "I thirst." They lift a sponge of sour wine to his mouth. And then three words in English, one in Greek: "It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost."
The Greek is tetelestai: finished, completed, accomplished, brought to its end.
Not I'm finished, as in defeated. It is finished, as in done, the work completed. Christians have long sung a Latin hymn about this scene called Stabat Mater, the mother was standing.
Because that's what she did. She couldn't stop it or fix it. She stood there.

how: On Good Friday, many churches read the Passion from John's Gospel, and some hold three hours of prayer and silence in the afternoon. The Stabat Mater is sung in many churches, and Catholics and others remember Our Lady of Sorrows.

o: I am finished: beaten and defeated at last
it is finished: a work brought to completion
it is beginning: the work is only starting

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: took her unto his own home

s: John's Gospel names the beloved disciple as John
the Gospel never names him. tradition has long said it was John.
from the cross, Jesus gave his mother and the beloved disciple to each other
woman, behold thy son. behold thy mother.
it is finished means I am defeated
tetelestai means completed, accomplished, brought to its end.

games.q: you're the beloved disciple, standing at the cross. Jesus looks at you and at his mother and says: behold thy mother. what do you do?
o: stay a while, then go home alone.
take her into your own home from that hour.
find her other relatives to care for her.
games.why: from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home. even on the cross, Jesus makes sure his mother isn't left alone.

practice: Think of someone who is suffering right now, sick, grieving, lonely, stuck, or just worn down; you probably can't fix it, and that's hard.
Instead of looking for the fix, picture simply being with them: sitting in the room, staying on the phone a little longer, not leaving when it gets uncomfortable, just staying.
If you pray, you can hold them before God without words.

wordCard.voice: Tetelestai. Jesus's last word from the cross in John's Gospel, one Greek word meaning it is finished: not defeat, but a work completed.

orig.note: Greek: it is finished, completed, brought to its end. One word, the last John records.

carryVoice: Your line: stay. Tomorrow, a garden, early, while it's still dark. Sixty-nine days now.
